stops.name: San Mateo, the capitulation
stops.campa: On 25 July 1812 Miranda signs the capitulation known to history as San Mateo: the republic surrenders on terms, persons and property guaranteed, passports for those who wish to leave, no persecutions. He signs to save the people from a war he can no longer win, spending his own glory as the last coin left. The officers around him cry treason; the canon answers that generals who cannot feed their armies do not own the luxury of last stands. Monteverde will honor nothing: every clause will be broken on the bodies of patriots, and the broken parchment becomes the Precursor's vindication.

stops.name: La Guaira, the night of 30–31 July: the parricide
stops.campa: Miranda sleeps at the house of Manuel María de las Casas in La Guaira, meaning to sail at dawn with the archive, to raise the cause again from abroad as he has all his life. At three in the morning of 31 July his own officers wake him with lanterns: Casas, Peña, and Simón Bolívar among those who seize him. He dresses without haste, holds the lantern to their faces, and speaks the sentence the nation will never stop hearing. The sworn son delivers the master to the Spaniards: the parricide of the revolution, the tragedy at the foundation of the house.
stops.quote: ¡Bochinche, bochinche! Esta gente no sabe hacer sino bochinche.
stops.quote_source: Palabras de Miranda en su arresto, La Guaira, madrugada del 31 de julio de 1812 (tradición unánime del canon; Robertson)

stops.name: La Guaira, Castillo San Carlos: the first dungeon
stops.campa: Casas closes the port on Monteverde's order and hands the Generalissimo to the Spaniard Cervériz, cruelest of the king's provosts. In the castle of San Carlos above La Guaira the man whose name is on the Arc de Triomphe is loaded with irons: thirty pounds of Spanish chain on the wrists that signed the capitulation guaranteeing every other man's liberty but his own. The officers who seized him receive their passports from Monteverde; Bolívar receives his and sails to begin his destiny. The master's chains are the price of the disciple's future: the canon states the exchange and lets it burn.

stops.name: Puerto Cabello, Castillo de San Felipe: the memorial
stops.campa: Transferred to the dungeons of San Felipe at Puerto Cabello, the very fortress whose loss wounded Venezuela in the heart, Miranda does from his cell the only thing left to a man of law and arms deprived of arms: he writes. On 8 March 1813 he addresses to the Real Audiencia of Caracas the great memorial demanding that Spain honor the capitulation it signed: the elderly, the clergy, persons of every class arrested without cause, buried in the vaults of La Guaira and Puerto Cabello. The prisoner argues the rights of his jailers' other victims. The Audiencia files it. The canon publishes it forever.
stops.quote: …a la autoridad de la Real Audiencia, en cuyas manos reside exclusiva y constitucionalmente el poder superior judiciario de este distrito, acudo…
stops.quote_source: Memorial de Miranda a la Real Audiencia de Caracas, Castillo de San Felipe de Puerto Cabello, 8 de marzo de 1813

stops.name: San Juan de Puerto Rico, El Morro
stops.campa: In June 1813, as Bolívar's Admirable Campaign sweeps back toward Caracas, Spain moves its great prisoner out of reach: Miranda is shipped in irons to the fortress of El Morro at San Juan de Puerto Rico. From a casemate over the Atlantic he watches the treasure fleets' old harbor and writes to London, to Washington, to anyone: the network of Grafton Street trying to pull its founder out of the stone. The empire, which could never defeat him at large, holds him now the only way it ever could: by the wrists. The next ship carries him to Spain itself.

stops.name: La Carraca, Cádiz: the arsenal prison of the Cuatro Torres
stops.campa: At the beginning of 1814 Miranda is landed at the arsenal of La Carraca, in the bay of Cádiz, and locked in the fort of the Cuatro Torres. The circle has closed: the harbor where the young captain of 1771 stepped ashore to serve the King now holds the old general who unmade the King's America. In Cádiz itself, across the water, the lodge of the Caballeros Racionales, daughter of Grafton Street, has already sworn its hundreds; the prisoner's doctrine walks free through the streets his body cannot reach. Beside his cot: the Plans, still, and the classics, and the flag folded in his memory.

stops.name: La Carraca, the escape prepared; the stroke
stops.campa: Two years in the Cuatro Torres: petitions to the restored Ferdinand answered with silence, the fetters loosened only by bribes, the old body failing while the mind keeps perfect order in its archive. Friends in Gibraltar and London raise money; a boat, a bribed sentry, a passage to England stand ready in the spring of 1816. Days before the hour, apoplexy strikes him down in his cell. The canon grieves the timing like a wound: liberty came for the Precursor once more, and found him already leaving by the older door.

stops.name: La Carraca, death on Bastille Day; the mass grave
stops.campa: In the first hours of 14 July 1816, Bastille Day, the day of the revolution whose arch bears his name, Francisco de Miranda dies in the prison of the Cuatro Torres, sixty-six years old, four years in chains. The arsenal buries him in the common grave of its cemetery, without stone or mark; the empire that could not answer his memorial answers his body with anonymity. It miscalculates one last time: a grave that is nowhere is a grave that is everywhere. The most travelled man of his age is issued, in death, the whole earth.

stops.name: Caracas, Panteón Nacional: the open cenotaph
stops.campa: The nation he invented builds him, in its Panteón, a tomb with the doors sculpted open: the cenotaph of Miranda, empty because Cádiz never yielded the bones, open because the country is still waiting. Above it his tricolor; around it the disciples: Bolívar under the altar, the sworn of Grafton Street in the aisles. In the canon the empty sarcophagus is not an absence but a commission: the Precursor's remains are the flag, the archive, the map of the journey itself, Caracas to La Carraca, the circle that a nation retraces every time it names its colors.
